# Diagnosing Dragging Brakes on a 2000 Chevy Silverado: Beyond the Caliper

When a vehicle sits parked and refuses to roll, or requires significant throttle input to move from a standstill, you are dealing with excessive hydraulic pressure holding the braking components engaged. The specific behavior describedâwhere jacking up the truck reveals that wheels will not turn, yet the rear wheels can be rotated with extreme force while the front wheels remain lockedâis a classic diagnostic puzzle in automotive repair. This scenario often leads owners to prematurely replace expensive components like calipers and rotors without isolating the root cause of the hydraulic lock.

The immediate suspicion usually falls on the newly installed hardware. Since the front passenger-side rotor and caliper were just replaced, it is logical to inspect that assembly first. However, if all four wheels exhibit locking behavior immediately after the repair, the issue likely lies upstream in the hydraulic circuit or within the new parts themselves. A dragging brake system feels like a software bug where a background process refuses to release; in this mechanical context, the "process" is the hydraulic fluid pressurizing the piston.

If the caliper slides are not moving freely, the caliper will remain clamped against the rotor regardless of the state of the master cylinder. When you replaced the caliper, verify that the guide pins were lubricated and that the slider bolts allow full retraction. If the new caliper was seized or installed with insufficient clearance for thermal expansion, it can act as a one-way valve for pressure, trapping fluid in the system. This explains why the truck drove fine for about a day; heat expands brake fluid, but once the vehicle cools and stops, the trapped air bubbles or fluid volume can create a hard lock-up that prevents wheel rotation when jacked up.

The master cylinder is rarely the culprit for total wheel locking unless there is an internal bypass failure or a blocked vent in the reservoir cap. While it is uncommon for a master cylinder to cause brakes to drag to the point of immobility immediately after installation, a clogged return passage inside the unit could prevent fluid from returning to the reservoir when the pedal is released. This creates a high-pressure state that mimics a stuck caliper. To diagnose this, remove the bleeder screw on the affected wheel cylinder or caliper and attempt to bleed the system while the vehicle is stationary. If fluid flows freely but the brakes still drag once reinstalled, the issue is mechanical within the caliper assembly, not hydraulic pressure generation.

Another critical factor is air entrapment during the bleeding process. Air bubbles compress under pedal pressure, leading to a spongy feel, but large pockets of air can also cause erratic pressure distribution where some wheels lock while others do not. The fact that the front wheels are completely unresponsive compared to the rear suggests a blockage or seizure specific to the front circuit. Before assuming the master cylinder is faulty, inspect the banjo bolts and flare connections on the brake lines for debris that could restrict flow. A tiny piece of metal shavings from the new rotor installation could lodge in the line, acting as a partial valve that opens under extreme force (when pushing with strength) but remains closed under normal driving conditions.

If you have verified the mechanical movement of the caliper pistons and confirmed the lines are clear, the next step is to isolate each wheel individually by disconnecting the brake line from the caliper. If the wheel turns freely when disconnected from the hydraulic system but locks up immediately upon reconnecting, the fault is definitively in the master cylinder or the specific line feeding that corner. In this rare case, flushing the entire system and replacing the master cylinder would be the necessary correction to restore normal braking dynamics.
